title: Our Verdict
text: Formal Data Generating Mechanisms, Likelihood Ratio Tests, 95% Confidence Intervals & Empirical Verdict

title: Our Verdict
text:
1. Data Generating Mechanism (DGM) Formulations
To predict individual educational attainment (\(Y_{\text{educ}}\)) conditioned on socio-demographic origin traits, we establish two formal statistical Data Generating Mechanisms: a primary Multinomial Logistic DGM for categorical milestone tiers and an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) DGM for continuous schooling years.

1.1 Multinomial Logistic DGM
We model the conditional log-odds of an individual attaining educational tier \(k \in \{\text{Some College}, \text{Bachelor Degree}, \text{Graduate Degree}\}\) relative to baseline \(K_0 = \text{High School or Less}\):
\[\ln\left(\frac{P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X})}{P(Y_{\text{educ}} = K_0 \mid \mathbf{X})}\right) = \beta_{k0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_k^T \mathbf{X}\]
where \(\mathbf{X}\) represents the vector of statistically selected socio-demographic covariates:
\[\mathbf{X} = \Big[ \text{parent\_educ}, \text{incom16}, \text{sibs}, \text{childs}, \text{age}, \text{year}, \text{sex}, \text{race}, \text{res16}, \text{family16}, \text{born}, \text{parborn} \Big]^T\]
The predicted conditional probability \(P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X})\) across all 4 attainment levels is determined via the soft-max transformation:
\[P(Y_{\text{educ}} = k \mid \mathbf{X}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_{k0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_k^T \mathbf{X}\right)}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{3} \exp\left(\beta_{j0} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_j^T \mathbf{X}\right)}\]



1.2 Linear Regression DGM
As a comparative benchmark, we model completed years of schooling (\(Y_{\text{years}} \in [0, 20]\)) as a continuous conditional expectation:
\[Y_{\text{years}} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}^T \mathbf{X} + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

title: Our Verdict
text:
5. Formal Predictive Verdict

📊 Predictive Modeling Verdict & Key Summary

1. Easy-to-Follow Model Accuracy Evaluation
To evaluate how accurately our model predicts educational outcomes, we test its performance across the \(N = 48,360\) survey respondents:

College Degree Prediction Accuracy (72.3%): When predicting whether an individual will successfully earn a Bachelor’s degree or higher versus a non-college path, our model achieves 72.3% overall accuracy.
What This Means in Plain English: Imagine taking a room of 100 people. By only looking at basic background information from their childhood—such as their parents’ education level, household income tier, family structure, and sibling count—our model correctly predicts whether 72 out of 100 people will graduate from college. In social science, where human decisions and personal choices vary widely, a 72.3% accuracy rate confirms that childhood background factors exert a dominant influence on lifetime educational attainment.



2. Answer to Central Predictive Question

“To what extent do social, economic, and demographic factors jointly predict whether an individual achieves a specific education level such as a Bachelor’s degree in the United States?”


Parental Education is the Single Strongest Predictor:

Accuracy & Effect Size: Every additional year of parental schooling increases an individual’s odds of earning a Bachelor’s degree by 33.3% (\(\text{OR} = 1.333\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[1.319, 1.348]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and a Graduate degree by 40.5% (\(\text{OR} = 1.405\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[1.388, 1.423]\), \(p < 0.001\)).
Continuous Schooling Impact: In the OLS linear model, each additional year of parental education directly increases completed schooling by +0.326 years (\(95\%\text{ CI: }[0.318, 0.333]\), \(p < 0.001\)).

Childhood Household Income & Family Dynamics:

Relative Household Income: Higher childhood relative income (incom16) significantly increases Bachelor’s degree completion odds by 16.8% per income tier (\(\text{OR} = 1.168\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[1.129, 1.209]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and adds +0.129 years of schooling (\(p < 0.001\)).
Single-Parent Family Structure: Growing up in a single-parent family reduces Bachelor’s degree odds by 43.8% (\(\text{OR} = 0.562\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[0.530, 0.596]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and reduces total completed schooling by -0.607 years (\(p < 0.001\)).
Sibling Size: Each additional sibling reduces Bachelor’s degree completion odds by 14.6% (\(\text{OR} = 0.854\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[0.840, 0.868]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and reduces schooling by -0.182 years per sibling (\(p < 0.001\)).

Geographic & Immigrant Origin Dynamics:

Suburban & Large City Origins: Growing up in a suburban environment increases Bachelor’s degree odds by 41.7% compared to rural origins (\(\text{OR} = 1.417\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[1.358, 1.479]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and adds +0.246 years of completed schooling.
Parental Immigrant Status: Children of immigrant parents whose parents were not born in the U.S. exhibit 77.1% higher odds of completing a Bachelor’s degree (\(\text{OR} = 1.771\), \(95\%\text{ CI: }[1.714, 1.830]\), \(p < 0.001\)) and gain +0.508 years of total schooling.




3. Strategic Policy Recommendation
Because parental education and childhood economic status exert strong conditional effects on educational outcomes, state policy initiatives should combine targeted higher education tuition subsidies with family support programs to foster intergenerational socio-economic mobility.

title: Our Question and Our Data
text: How parental background, childhood economic environment, family structure, geography, and birth cohorts shape individual educational outcomes.

title: Our Question and Our Data
text:
1. The Context
Educational attainment is one of the most vital determinants of individual socio-economic mobility, health outcomes, and lifelong earnings trajectory in modern society. Over the past five decades, access to post-secondary education has expanded dramatically across the United States. However, individual educational trajectories remain deeply embedded within socio-demographic origins, parental academic background, and so much more.
Understanding how these background factors jointly influence educational attainment enables workforce policy planners, academic leaders, and sociologists to quantify intergenerational mobility and identify structural barriers to higher education.

title: Our Question and Our Data
text:
2. Central Predictive Research Question
To what extent do social, economic, and demographic factors jointly predict whether an individual achieves a specific education level such as a Bachelor’s degree in the United States?

title: Data Sources & References
text:
1. Primary Empirical Data Source
The empirical analysis in this project is based on data from the General Social Survey (GSS), conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago.

General Social Survey (NORC at the University of Chicago)

Reference List Citation: > Davern, M., Bautista, R., Freese, J., Herd, P., & Morgan, S. L. (2024). General Social Survey 1972–2024 (Release 3) [Data set]. NORC at the University of Chicago. https://gssdataexplorer.norc.org
Dataset Scope & Methodology: The General Social Survey (GSS) is one of the nation’s most authoritative, long-running social science research studies. Since 1972, the GSS has monitored societal trends and demographic transformations across the adult, non-institutionalized population of the United States using nationally representative probability sampling.

title: Data Sources & References
text:
2. Variable Codebook & Descriptions
Below are the official GSS codebook definitions for all 15 variables analyzed in this study:








Variable Name
GSS Label
Description & Coding Scheme




educ
Respondent Educational Attainment
Highest grade of school completed (0–20 years). Recoded into 4 tiers: High School or Less, Some College, Bachelor Degree, Graduate Degree.


paeduc
Father’s Educational Attainment
Highest grade of school completed by respondent’s father (0–20 years).


maeduc
Mother’s Educational Attainment
Highest grade of school completed by respondent’s mother (0–20 years).


incom16
Relative Family Income at Age 16
Family income at age 16 relative to American families: 1 = Far Below Average, 2 = Below Average, 3 = Average, 4 = Above Average, 5 = Far Above Average.


family16
Family Structure at Age 16
Living arrangement at age 16: Both Own Parents, Single Parent, Stepparent, Other Relative/Arrangement.


res16
Residence Type at Age 16
Type of place lived in at age 16: Farm, Country Non-Farm, Town <50k, 50k to 250k, Big-City Suburb, City >250k.


sex
Respondent’s Sex
Sex assigned at interview: Female, Male.


race
Respondent’s Race
Race of respondent: White, Black, Other.


born
Respondent Born in U.S.
Was the respondent born in the United States? Yes, No.


parborn
Parents Born in U.S.
Were respondent’s parents born in the U.S.? Both U.S., One U.S., Neither U.S.


sibs
Number of Siblings
Total number of brothers and sisters (0 to 6+).


childs
Number of Children
Ever had children / total number of children (0 to 8+).


age
Respondent’s Age
Age at time of interview (18 to 89 years).


year
Survey Administration Year
Calendar year of survey round (1972 through 2024).


agekdbrn
Age at First Child’s Birth
Age when respondent’s first child was born. (Excluded from final predictive model due to 62.1% missingness/inapplicability across historical survey rounds).
